newsitem.title: USA: U.S authorities step up search for missing airmen.
newsitem.headline: U.S authorities step up search for missing airmen.

text.p: Authorities stepped up the search on Saturday for survivors or victims of a U.S. Air Force Reserve transport plane with 11 people on board that plunged into the Pacific Ocean after reporting engine trouble.

Coast Guard, military and civilian aircraft and ships searched throughout the night for crew members of the HC-130 Hercules which crashed about 60 miles (95 kms) off Cape Mendocino on the northern California coast on Friday evening.
A Coast Guard helicopter pulled one survivor to safety late on Friday and one body has been recovered, the Coast Guard said.
Coast Guard Lieutenant Joe Pesci said earlier that rescuers had spotted several bodies they had not yet been able to recover among the wreckage, which was spread over a wide area.
Daylight made the task easier for the searchers, hampered earlier by pitch darkness. With visibility of 12 miles (20 kms) and short, choppy seas, search conditions were described as moderate.
The searchers were scouring a huge 108 square mile (170 square km) area for possible survivors, Coast Guard spokesman Chief Petty Officer Ronald Cabral said.
"They should find something today," Cabral said. He said "there's always hope" of finding more survivors. Other officials said hypothermia was a danger for anyone spending so long in the cold water.
Search efforts were intensified with two Air Force helicopters and an Air Force C-130 from Moffett Field in California joining Coast Guard units, Cabral said.
A Coast Guard cutter and a Navy destroyer were involved in the search together with a merchant ship and a private fishing boat, Cabral said. Another Coast Guard cutter was on its way.

The hulking four-engined aircraft, a military workhorse, was flying from Portland Air Base to San Diego, California on a routine training mission when crew members reported they had shut down one engine and also had electrical problems, Air Force spokeswoman Karole Scott said from Portland, where the aircraft was based.
Soon afterwards, air traffic controllers in Oakland and Seattle lost radar and radio contact, she said.
The Coast Guard's Pesci said the crew had told authorities it planned to turn towards land for a precautionary landing just before contact was lost.

The rescued airman, Technical Sgt. Robert Vogel, a 31-year-old airborne communications specialist from Albany, Oregon, was flown to a California hospital where he was listed in stable condition, the Air Force said.
The names of the missing airmen were not disclosed.
Scott said the families of the crew members had all been notified they were missing. "They are being supported by our officers," she said.

Coast Guard officials said the crew's chances of survival were better than an average person's because they were trained in survival techniques and wore flight suits that would help keep them warm in the cold water.
The plane was assigned to the 939th Rescue Wing's 304th Rescue Squadron, the Air Force said. In war time, the unit's mission is combat rescue behind enemy lines, Scott said.
Scott said the Air Force would convene an accident board to investigate the cause of the crash.
